merchant-cash-advance.summary: A factor rate of 1.30 on a $50,000 advance means $65,000 of contracted remittances. With a $1,500 withheld fee, the business receives $48,500 and pays $16,500 more than that net funding. Annualized cost also depends on the actual remittance dates.
merchant-cash-advance.scope: One USD factor-based advance; one fee withheld at funding; all remittances later than funding. Fixed count or constant eligible-sales/holdback scenario, actual calendar dates and Actual/365 effective annual IRR. At most 1,000 remittances /3,650 days; IRR above 1,000,000% flagged. No legal APR, state disclosures, variable-sales forecast, extra fees, refinancing or actual contract reconciliation.

examples.title: Reconcile gross advance, withheld fee and total cash cost
examples.inputs: advance: 50000; factor: 1.3; withheld_fees: 1500; funding_date: 2026-12-01; first_debit: 2026-12-02; calendar: Weekdays (Mon–Fri only); remittances: 130
steps: 50,000 × 1.30 = 65,000 contracted remittances.
Cash cost = 65,000 − 48,500 = 16,500; the factor markup alone is only 15,000.
examples.answer: Total financing cash cost above net funding: 16,500.00 under these assumptions.

expected.label: Total financing cash cost above net funding

examples.title: Annualize the explicit weekday remittance dates
examples.inputs: advance: 50000; factor: 1.3; withheld_fees: 1500; funding_date: 2026-12-01; first_debit: 2026-12-02; calendar: Weekdays (Mon–Fri only); remittances: 130
steps: The 130 remittances are 500 each, beginning December 2 after December 1 funding.
Skip weekends only, then discount each dated outflow on an Actual/365 basis.
The resulting compounded effective annual IRR is not the 30% factor markup or a legal APR.
examples.answer: Illustrative effective annual IRR, not legal APR: 243.3222% under these assumptions.

expected.label: Illustrative effective annual IRR, not legal APR

examples.title: Match a 10% holdback to 5,000 eligible sales per interval
examples.inputs: advance: 50000; factor: 1.3; withheld_fees: 1500; funding_date: 2026-12-01; first_debit: 2026-12-02; calendar: Weekdays (Mon–Fri only); sales_per_interval: 5000; holdback: 10
steps: 5,000 × 10% = 500 per eligible interval.
65,000 / 500 = 130 assumed remittances at constant sales.
examples.answer: Assumed number of remittances: 130.00 under these assumptions.

examples.title: Reduce the final remittance to the remaining contract amount
examples.inputs: advance: 1000; factor: 1.3; withheld_fees: 0; funding_date: 2026-12-01; first_debit: 2026-12-02; calendar: Weekdays (Mon–Fri only); sales_per_interval: 3000; holdback: 10
steps: Contracted total is 1,300 and normal remittances are 300.
Four normal remittances total 1,200; the fifth is only 100.
examples.answer: Final scheduled remittance: 100.00 under these assumptions.

examples.title: Extend the scenario when eligible sales are lower
examples.inputs: advance: 50000; factor: 1.3; withheld_fees: 1500; funding_date: 2026-12-01; first_debit: 2026-12-02; calendar: Weekdays (Mon–Fri only); sales_per_interval: 2500; holdback: 10
steps: 2,500 × 10% = 250 per interval.
The unchanged 65,000 total requires 260 remittances. Actual revenue is not forecast.
examples.answer: Assumed number of remittances: 260.00 under these assumptions.

examples.title: Keep zero financing cost at a 1.00 factor with no fee
examples.inputs: advance: 50000; factor: 1; withheld_fees: 0; funding_date: 2026-12-01; first_debit: 2026-12-02; calendar: Weekdays (Mon–Fri only); remittances: 130
steps: Net funding and total remittances are both 50,000.
Every future remittance discounts to the funding total at a zero rate.
examples.answer: Illustrative effective annual IRR, not legal APR: 0.0000% under these assumptions.

expected.label: Illustrative effective annual IRR, not legal APR

questions.question: Is a factor rate of 1.30 the same as 30% APR?
questions.answer: No. It sets a 30% markup on the gross advance in this model. Annualized cash-flow cost also depends on net funding, remittance timing and amount.

questions.question: Does a slower sales assumption reduce the contract total?
questions.answer: No. It lengthens the constant-sales scenario while the entered factor still determines the same remittance total. Actual contract reconciliation rules are outside the model.

questions.question: Are bank holidays skipped?
questions.answer: No. The weekday calendar skips Saturday and Sunday only. The first remittance is entered explicitly; a contract-specific calendar can differ.

backdoor-roth-ira.summary: A backdoor Roth conversion is not automatically tax-free. With $7,500 established nondeductible basis, $92,500 left in included IRAs at year end and $7,500 converted, the ordinary pool is $100,000. Only $562.50 of the conversion is nontaxable; $6,937.50 is taxable.
backdoor-roth-ira.scope: U.S. 2026 ordinary individual traditional-IRA pro-rata allocation using established nondeductible basis, aggregated included December 31 IRA values, eligible outstanding IRA-to-IRA rollovers, conversions and other included distributions. Following-year contributions excluded from current allocation but retained in basis. Published 2026 Form 8606; 2025 instructions for context. No contribution/deduction eligibility engine, special adjustments, inherited/mega-backdoor plan, penalties, five-year withdrawal or full-return calculation.

examples.title: Allocate basis across existing IRA balances
examples.inputs: case_scope: Ordinary case; basis confirmed; prior_basis: 0; current_nondeductible: 7500; year_end_iras: 92500; outstanding_rollovers: 0; converted: 7500; assumed_rate: 24
steps: Pool = 92,500 year-end values + 7,500 conversion = 100,000.
7,500 / 100,000 = 7.5% nontaxable fraction; conversion basis is 562.50.
Taxable conversion = 7,500 − 562.50 = 6,937.50.
examples.answer: Taxable portion of 2026 Roth conversions: 6,937.50 under these assumptions.

examples.title: Convert with no other included year-end IRA value
examples.inputs: case_scope: Ordinary case; basis confirmed; prior_basis: 0; current_nondeductible: 7500; year_end_iras: 0; outstanding_rollovers: 0; converted: 7500; assumed_rate: 24
steps: Basis and the conversion pool are both 7,500.
The fraction is capped at 100%, so the conversion is nontaxable under this ordinary case.
examples.answer: Taxable portion of 2026 Roth conversions: 0.00 under these assumptions.

examples.title: Keep growth above nondeductible basis taxable
examples.inputs: case_scope: Ordinary case; basis confirmed; prior_basis: 0; current_nondeductible: 7500; year_end_iras: 0; outstanding_rollovers: 0; converted: 7600; assumed_rate: 24
steps: Basis is 7,500 but 7,600 is converted after assumed growth.
The conversion uses 7,500 of basis, leaving 100 taxable.
examples.answer: Taxable portion of 2026 Roth conversions: 100.00 under these assumptions.

examples.title: Exclude an early-2027 contribution from the 2026 allocation
examples.inputs: case_scope: Ordinary case; basis confirmed; prior_basis: 0; current_nondeductible: 7500; year_end_iras: 92500; outstanding_rollovers: 0; converted: 7500; assumed_rate: 24; next_year_contribution: 7500; other_distributions: 0
steps: All 7,500 of the 2026 contribution was made in early 2027.
With no prior basis, eligible 2026 allocation basis is zero; the 7,500 conversion is taxable.
The 7,500 contribution remains in total carryforward basis.
examples.answer: Taxable portion of 2026 Roth conversions: 7,500.00 under these assumptions.

examples.title: Share basis once across conversion and other included distributions
examples.inputs: case_scope: Ordinary case; basis confirmed; prior_basis: 0; current_nondeductible: 7500; year_end_iras: 82500; outstanding_rollovers: 0; converted: 7500; assumed_rate: 24; next_year_contribution: 0; other_distributions: 10000
steps: Pool = 82,500 + 7,500 converted + 10,000 other distributions = 100,000.
Basis used = 562.50 on conversion + 750 on other distributions = 1,312.50.
Carryforward basis = 7,500 − 1,312.50 = 6,187.50.
examples.answer: Remaining IRA basis after 2026 allocation: 6,187.50 under these assumptions.

examples.title: Include established basis carried from earlier years
examples.inputs: case_scope: Ordinary case; basis confirmed; prior_basis: 2500; current_nondeductible: 7500; year_end_iras: 90000; outstanding_rollovers: 0; converted: 10000; assumed_rate: 24
steps: Total eligible basis = 2,500 prior + 7,500 current = 10,000.
The 100,000 pool produces a 10% nontaxable fraction, so 9,000 of the conversion is taxable.
examples.answer: Taxable portion of 2026 Roth conversions: 9,000.00 under these assumptions.

examples.title: Preserve basis when only part of a basis-only pool is converted
examples.inputs: case_scope: Ordinary case; basis confirmed; prior_basis: 0; current_nondeductible: 7500; year_end_iras: 3750; outstanding_rollovers: 0; converted: 3750; assumed_rate: 24
steps: A 7,500 basis-only pool has 3,750 converted and 3,750 remaining.
The conversion is nontaxable and uses 3,750 basis, leaving 3,750 carried forward.
examples.answer: Remaining IRA basis after 2026 allocation: 3,750.00 under these assumptions.

questions.question: Can I convert only the after-tax money in a new IRA?
questions.answer: The ordinary allocation uses the individual’s aggregate included IRA pool, not an account label. A separate new IRA does not by itself isolate basis.

questions.question: Does the calculator decide how much I may contribute?
questions.answer: No. Enter a contribution amount already determined eligible and nondeductible. The tax rate is also your supplied incremental assumption, not a bracket calculation.

questions.question: Does leftover basis disappear after a conversion?
questions.answer: No. This worksheet subtracts basis used on the conversion and other included distributions once, retaining the unused total, including the following-year contribution portion.
